seo_title: Ordinance and Law Coverage Explained for Texas Owners
meta_description: Ordinance and law coverage explained: how code upgrade costs are paid after a Texas property loss and how to protect your claim.
h1: Ordinance and Law Coverage Explained: Paying for Code Upgrades
secondary_keywords: coverage A B C ordinance or law
excerpt: Rebuilding to current code can cost far more than a straight repair. Learn how ordinance and law coverage works, what it pays, and how Texas owners avoid disputes.
key_takeaways: Ordinance and law coverage pays extra costs to rebuild to current building code after a covered loss.
It usually has three parts: undamaged portion, demolition, and increased cost of construction.
Many policies pay code upgrade costs only after the work is completed.
Permits and building department records are your strongest proof of required upgrades.
Appraisal can settle what code work costs, but not whether coverage exists.
body_html:
Ordinance and law coverage pays the extra cost of rebuilding to current building codes after a covered loss. It typically covers three things: the undamaged part of a building that code forces you to tear down, the demolition and debris cost, and the increased cost of construction. Without it, code upgrades often come out of your pocket.

What is ordinance and law coverage?

A standard property policy pays to repair or replace what was damaged with materials of like kind and quality. The problem is that "like kind" is measured against what was there before the storm, fire or leak. If your home or building was constructed under an older code, rebuilding it the same way may no longer be legal.

Ordinance and law coverage (sometimes written "ordinance or law") fills that gap. It responds when a city, county or state rule requires work that goes beyond a straight replacement. Common examples include new roof underlayment or drip edge requirements, electrical and plumbing upgrades, accessibility features in commercial buildings, energy code items, and engineered wind-resistance details on the Texas coast.

The key point: this coverage only applies when the code upgrade is triggered by a covered loss. It does not pay to modernize a building that was never damaged.

The three parts of ordinance and law coverage

Most commercial forms, and many homeowners endorsements, divide the coverage into three parts. Insurers and agents often call them Coverage A, B and C. Knowing which part applies to your loss makes it far easier to read an estimate and spot what is missing.

PartWhat it pays forTypical example
Coverage A: Loss to the undamaged portionThe value of the undamaged part of a building that must be demolished because of codeA city requires full demolition once damage passes a set threshold, even though half the structure was untouched
Coverage B: Demolition costTearing down and hauling away the undamaged portion that code requires removingDebris removal for walls that were structurally fine but cannot legally stay
Coverage C: Increased cost of constructionThe added cost of rebuilding to current code compared with rebuilding the old wayNew underlayment, upgraded electrical panels, larger egress windows, wind-rated fastening

In homeowner claims, Coverage C is the part that shows up most often. In commercial claims, all three can matter, especially after a fire or a major wind event that damages a large share of the building.

Does my homeowners policy include ordinance and law coverage?

It depends on the form and the endorsements you bought. Many homeowners policies include a limited amount of ordinance and law coverage, often expressed as a percentage of the dwelling limit. Others exclude it unless you add an endorsement. Commercial property policies usually require a separate ordinance or law endorsement with its own limits.

To find out what you have, check these places in your policy:

  • Declarations page: look for an "ordinance or law" line item, a percentage, or an endorsement number.
  • Additional coverages section: many homeowners forms list a code-upgrade allowance here.
  • Exclusions: look for language excluding loss caused by "enforcement of any ordinance or law."
  • Endorsements: commercial policies may list separate limits for Coverage A, B and C, or a single combined limit.
Tip: If your declarations show a percentage, multiply it by your dwelling limit to see the actual dollar ceiling. A small percentage can disappear quickly on an older home that needs a new roof system and electrical work.

How ordinance and law coverage works in a claim

Ordinance and law items are often handled differently from the rest of the estimate. Understanding the sequence helps you avoid leaving money on the table.

  1. The covered loss is identified. The carrier must first accept that the underlying damage is covered.
  2. Code requirements are confirmed. Your contractor, the local building department or the permit itself shows what the current code requires.
  3. Code items are priced separately. In a well-written Xactimate or Symbility estimate, code-required items are usually identified so the adjuster can apply the correct coverage.
  4. Payment may be held until the work is done. Many policies pay increased cost of construction only when the repair is actually completed, similar to how recoverable depreciation is released after repairs.
  5. Limits apply. Ordinance and law payments are capped by their own limit, separate from or carved out of the dwelling limit.

Because payment is often tied to completion, keep permits, inspection records and invoices. They are the proof that the code work was required and that it was performed.

An illustrative example

Say hail destroys the shingles on a 1990s home and the carrier's estimate is $16,000 for a like-for-like roof. The city now requires drip edge and a different underlayment, and several sheets of decking no longer meet fastening requirements. Those items might add a few thousand dollars. If the policy includes ordinance and law coverage, that added cost should be paid up to the applicable limit, often after the work is completed. If the policy excludes it, the owner may bear that cost personally. The numbers here are only an example, but the pattern is common.

Common code upgrades in Texas property claims

Texas does not have one statewide residential building code that every city enforces the same way. Many cities adopt versions of the International Residential Code and International Building Code, sometimes with local amendments. That means the same roof replacement can carry different code items in Austin, Dallas or Lubbock.

Roofing

Roof claims are where most Texas homeowners first meet ordinance and law issues. Depending on the adopted code and the manufacturer's installation requirements, an estimate may need to include drip edge, specific underlayment, starter strips, proper ventilation, or replacement of decking that no longer meets spacing or fastening requirements. Carrier estimates frequently leave these out, which is one reason we wrote a separate guide on Xactimate line items commonly missing from roof claims.

Coastal wind requirements

Along the Gulf Coast, the Texas Department of Insurance runs a windstorm inspection program for the designated catastrophe area. Structures that need certification for Texas Windstorm Insurance Association eligibility generally must be built or repaired to applicable windstorm standards, which can add fastening, connector and opening-protection costs. The TDI windstorm program pages explain the inspection and certification process. Property owners in Galveston, Corpus Christi and the Houston area should pay close attention to this.

Electrical, plumbing and accessibility

After fire and water losses, opening walls can trigger electrical upgrades such as arc-fault protection, smoke and carbon monoxide detector requirements, or plumbing changes. For commercial buildings, major renovations can bring accessibility requirements into play. Each of these may fall under Coverage C.

Why ordinance and law claims get disputed

Even when a policy clearly includes the coverage, disagreements are common. The most frequent reasons we see:

  • The upgrade was never included. The carrier's estimate prices a like-for-like repair and leaves code items off entirely.
  • The carrier questions whether code actually requires it. Without a permit, a building official's letter or code citation, the item may be denied.
  • Disagreement over how much work is triggered. For example, whether a partial repair can be done without triggering a full system upgrade, which overlaps with matching issues in insurance claims.
  • Pricing disputes. The carrier agrees the item belongs but prices it below what local contractors charge.
  • Limit confusion. Owners assume the dwelling limit covers code work, then discover a much smaller ordinance and law cap.

Can appraisal resolve ordinance and law disputes?

Often, yes, at least for part of the dispute. The appraisal clause in most Texas policies lets either side demand appraisal when they disagree on the amount of loss. Under State Farm Lloyds v. Johnson (Tex. 2009), Texas appraisers decide the amount of loss and may consider damage and causation, but they do not decide coverage.

In practice, that means appraisal works well when the question is "what does the code-required work cost?" or "how many squares of decking need replacement?" It is less suited to a pure coverage question, such as whether the policy includes ordinance and law coverage at all. Many appraisal awards separate code items into their own line so the carrier can apply the correct coverage afterward. If you are new to the process, start with what an insurance appraisal is and how the clause works.

This is general information, not legal advice. Coverage interpretation questions may call for a Texas attorney.

How to protect your ordinance and law recovery

A few practical steps make a real difference:

  1. Review your limits before storm season. Ask your agent what percentage or dollar amount applies and whether it is enough for an older property.
  2. Get code requirements in writing. Permits, inspection reports and building department correspondence carry weight with adjusters and appraisers.
  3. Ask for a line-item estimate. A detailed estimate that flags code items makes it harder for them to be overlooked.
  4. Track completion deadlines. Policies often set a time limit to complete repairs before held-back amounts are paid. Our recoverable depreciation calculator helps you see how much is still owed after the work is done.
  5. Do not accept "not covered" without reading the form. Ask the adjuster to identify the exact policy language they are relying on.

Next steps if code upgrades were left out

If your carrier's estimate prices a repair the old way and ignores what your city now requires, you may be absorbing costs your policy was designed to pay. Start by comparing the estimate against your permit and your contractor's scope, then ask the adjuster in writing to address each missing code item.

When the gap is significant and the carrier will not move, appraisal is often the most direct path to a fair number on the amount of loss. faqs.q: Is ordinance and law coverage included in a standard Texas homeowners policy?
faqs.a: Some Texas homeowners policies include a limited amount, often a percentage of the dwelling limit, while others require an endorsement. Check your declarations page, the additional coverages section and any endorsements. If you cannot find it, ask your agent in writing what code upgrade coverage applies and what the dollar limit is.

faqs.q: Does ordinance and law coverage pay for drip edge on a roof claim?
faqs.a: It can, if the locally adopted code requires drip edge and the roof replacement results from a covered loss. Some carriers also include drip edge as part of the normal replacement cost when manufacturer instructions require it. Either way, a permit or code citation from your city helps support the line item on the estimate.

faqs.q: When does an insurer pay increased cost of construction?
faqs.a: Many policies pay increased cost of construction only after the code-required work is actually completed, and sometimes only if it is done within a set time. Keep invoices, permits and final inspection records, then submit them to the carrier promptly so the held-back amount can be released under your policy terms.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Coverage A, B and C in ordinance or law?
faqs.a: Coverage A pays for the undamaged part of a building that code requires you to demolish. Coverage B pays the cost of that demolition and debris removal. Coverage C pays the increased cost of rebuilding to current code compared with rebuilding the way the structure was originally built. Limits may be separate or combined.

faqs.q: Can I use appraisal if my insurer underpaid code upgrades?
faqs.a: Yes, when the dispute is about the amount of loss, such as how much code-required work costs or how much decking needs replacing. In Texas, appraisers decide amount of loss but not coverage. Awards often list code items separately so the carrier can apply the correct coverage and limit afterward.
